Appendix E
Hallucination Analysis
To assess the quality and accuracy of the summarizations within our RAPTOR model, we conducted an analysis focusing on hallucinations in the generated summaries. The summaries were generated by
gpt-3.5-turbo
and subsequently annotated to quantify the rates of hallucinations, to examine whether such inaccuracies propagate to parent nodes, and to evaluate their impact on question-answering (QA) tasks.
E.1
Methodology
We randomly sampled 150 nodes across 40 stories and evaluated them for hallucinations. This sampling strategy provides a broad view of the model’s performance across different contexts. Each node was annotated by hand, and determined if it contained a hallucination.
E.2
Findings
Out of the 150 nodes sampled, 4% (6 nodes) contained some form of hallucination. Most commonly, these hallucinations originated from the model adding minor information possibly from its training data that was not present in the text being summarized, or from incorrectly extrapolating some information when creating the summary.
Example:
Text of the child nodes:
”And you will come with me to my people? We may live here among them, and you will be a great warrior–oh, when Jor dies you may even be chief, for there is none so mighty as my warrior…”But your father will not permit it–Jor, my father, High Chief of the Galus, will not permit it, for like me you are cos-ata-lo. Oh, Co-Tan, if we but could!… Bradley noticed that she spoke in English–broken English like Co-Tan’s but equally appealing.
Summary found in the parent of that node:
The protagonist, Bradley, is being asked by Co-Tan to stay with her people and become a great warrior, but he refuses and must return to his own country. Tom Billings of Santa Monica arrives and tells them he came to search for a man named Bowen J. Tyler, Jr. Ajor, Co-Tan’s sister, is excited about the possibility of going to Tom’s country to see strange and wonderful things…
The hallucination here is that the summary states that Jr. Ajor and Co-Tan are sisters, but does not explicitly mention or imply this.
Upon reviewing all parent nodes, we found that hallucinations did not propagate to higher layers. Generally, the hallucinations were minor and did not alter the thematic interpretation of the text.
E.3
Impact on QA Tasks
In our findings, hallucinations had no discernible impact on the performance of QA tasks. This suggests that hallucination is not a major concerns for the summarization component in our RAPTOR architecture.

Added Smoothing:
Smoothing was incorporated to handle cases where BLEU score is zero, due to no n-gram matches occurring in the reference text. A BLEU score of zero skews the results, leading to an overly harsh evaluation for rare or novel phrases. By adding a smoothing function, we prevent the BLEU scores from dropping to zero, providing a more fair evaluation.
•
Modified BLEU-4 Weighting:
The original script applied a weight of 1 to the highest order n-gram (4-gram) and 0 to the rest in its BLEU-4 calculation (i.e., weights=(0, 0, 0, 1)). This approach may overly focus on 4-gram matches while neglecting lower-order matches. To provide a more balanced evaluation, we evenly distributed the weight across all n-gram levels, changing the weights for the BLEU-4 calculation to (0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25).
•
Tokenization before Mapping in METEOR Calculation:
The original script utilized a simple split and map method for METEOR calculation. We fixed this by first tokenizing the text and then mapping the tokens. This amendment improves the accuracy of the METEOR calculation by taking into account the correct linguistic boundaries of words.

summaries.summary:
RAPTOR is a retrieval method described in one source, the arXiv paper "RAPTOR: Recursive Abstractive Processing for Tree-Organized Retrieval" (source_id: raptor, https://arxiv.org/html/2401.18059v1, dated 31 Jan 2024). The paper reports that RAPTOR builds a tree of text summaries. It starts with short text chunks of about 100 tokens. It embeds each chunk with SBERT. It groups similar chunks with a soft clustering method based on Gaussian Mixture Models. It summarizes each group with gpt-3.5-turbo. It repeats this process to make higher layers. At query time, it retrieves nodes from the tree. The paper reports two query methods: tree traversal and collapsed tree. In tests on 20 QASPER stories, collapsed tree with 2000 tokens gave the best result, so the authors used it for the main experiments. The paper reports that RAPTOR scales linearly in build time and token cost, tested on an Apple M1 Mac with 16GB RAM for documents from 12,500 to 78,000 tokens.

The paper reports controlled comparisons. With UnifiedQA 3B as the reader, RAPTOR improved results over the same retriever without RAPTOR on NarrativeQA, QASPER and QuALITY. On QASPER F-1, RAPTOR scored 53.1 with GPT-3, 55.7 with GPT-4 and 36.6 with UnifiedQA. The paper says these scores are higher than DPR by 1.8, 2.7 and 4.5 points, and higher than BM25 by 6.5, 5.5 and 10.2 points. On QuALITY accuracy, RAPTOR scored 62.4 with GPT-3 and 56.6 with UnifiedQA. The paper says this is at least 2.0 points above DPR and BM25. On NarrativeQA, RAPTOR with UnifiedQA reached ROUGE-L 30.8, BLEU-1 23.5, BLEU-4 6.4 and METEOR 19.1. The paper reports a new state of the art METEOR score for this setting. The paper also reports that RAPTOR with GPT-4 reached 55.7 F-1 on QASPER, above CoLT5 XL at 53.9, and 82.6 accuracy on the QuALITY test set, above CoLISA at 62.3. On the QuALITY-HARD subset, RAPTOR with GPT-4 scored 76.2, which the paper says is 21.5 points above CoLISA.

The paper reports an ablation on the clustering step. On QuALITY, RAPTOR with SBERT and UnifiedQA scored 56.6%, while a recency-based tree with the same embeddings and reader scored 55.8%. The paper reports that about 4% of sampled summaries contained minor hallucinations. It says these did not spread to parent nodes and had no clear effect on question answering. The paper reports that 18.5% to 57% of retrieved nodes came from non-leaf layers, depending on dataset and retriever. It reports that full-tree search beat searches limited to single layers in the story examples it tested. The paper states that the code will be released publicly. These are the paper's own reported results and claims, not independent verification.

The evidence is three separate documentation pages. Each page is a single original document. No source corroborates another, so treat every statement as a report from one source only. The three sources are: the psycopg 3.3.7.dev1 page "Connection pools" (source_id: pooling, https://www.psycopg.org/psycopg3/docs/advanced/pool.html); the PostgreSQL 18 page "19.3. Connections and Authentication" (source_id: postgres, https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html); and the Microsoft Learn page "PgBouncer in Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server" (source_id: azure, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/postgresql/connectivity/concepts-pgbouncer), last updated 2026-10-03.

All three sources describe connection pooling, but at different layers. The pooling source describes a client-side pool in the psycopg_pool package: it keeps between min_size and max_size connections, hands a ready connection to a caller at once, and makes other callers wait in a queue. A background worker creates new connections. On return, an open transaction is committed on normal exit or rolled back on an exception. A broken connection, or one older than max_lifetime, is discarded and replaced. The pool does not actively check idle connections, so a client can get a broken connection unless check is configured; ConnectionPool.check_connection is a simple check. A pool can be fixed size (no max_size, or max_size = min_size) or dynamic (max_size > min_size). Failed attempts retry with exponential backoff up to reconnect_timeout, then reconnect_failed() is called if given. Connections above min_size close one at a time after max_idle. The page says the right pool size is an open question and suggests get_stats() to monitor and resize() to change size at runtime. NullConnectionPool (added in version 3.1) creates no connection beforehand; returned connections close unless other clients wait. SQLAlchemy integration arrived in version 3.3, where close_returns makes close() return a connection to the pool. The open parameter currently defaults to True, but the page warns this may change to False, so code that relies on opening at creation should pass open=True. Opening an async pool in the constructor is deprecated. The pool logs to the psycopg.pool logger, and the page warns those messages are not a stable interface. get_stats() and pop_stats() return the same values, but pop_stats() resets counters. Metrics include pool_min, pool_max, pool_size, pool_available, requests_waiting, usage_ms, requests_num, requests_queued, requests_wait_ms, requests_errors, returns_bad, connections_num, connections_ms, connections_errors and connections_lost; keys with value 0 may be omitted and the set may change. A worked example uses min_size=2 and four worker threads, with printed timestamps from 2023-09-20 11:02:39 to 11:02:41. My inference: that example shows two connections serving four one-second tasks in two waves, which fits the page's statement that waiting clients can be served an existing connection when another client finishes first. The page itself does not state that conclusion.

The postgres source describes server-side connection limits and authentication, not a pool. listen_addresses defaults to localhost, so only local loopback connections work; an empty list means no IP interface and only Unix-domain sockets; * means all IP interfaces; 0.0.0.0 means all IPv4 addresses; :: means all IPv6 addresses. port defaults to 5432 and is the same for all IP addresses. max_connections defaults to typically 100, but can be lower if kernel settings do not support it, as determined during initdb. PostgreSQL sizes some resources, including shared memory, directly from max_connections. On a standby server, max_connections must be equal to or higher than on the primary, or queries are not allowed on the standby. reserved_connections defaults to zero and must be less than max_connections minus superuser_reserved_connections. superuser_reserved_connections defaults to three and must be less than max_connections minus reserved_connections. unix_socket_directories defaults to normally /tmp but can change at build time; on Windows the default is empty, so no Unix-domain socket is created by default. A value starting with @ creates a socket in the abstract namespace, currently supported on Linux only. unix_socket_permissions defaults to 0777, meaning anyone can connect; reasonable alternatives are 0770 (user and group) and 0700 (user only). For a Unix-domain socket, only write permission matters, and this access control is independent of the authentication rules in Chapter 20. authentication_timeout defaults to one minute (1m). password_encryption defaults to scram-sha-256; the other value is md5. The page warns that older clients might lack SCRAM support and therefore not work with SCRAM-SHA-256 passwords, and that MD5-encrypted password support is deprecated and will be removed in a future release. scram_iterations defaults to 4096; a higher number gives more protection against brute-force attacks on stored passwords but makes authentication slower. Changing the value has no effect on existing passwords, because the iteration count is fixed at the time of encryption; a new password must be set to use a changed value. The page notes that if a role password was created with a different iteration count than the value in postgresql.conf or on the server command line, an unauthenticated user can discern the existence of the role by observing differences in the server's responses to connection attempts. md5_password_warnings defaults to on. krb_server_keyfile defaults to FILE:/usr/local/pgsql/etc/krb5.keytab, where the directory part is whatever was specified as sysconfdir at build time. krb_caseins_users defaults to off, meaning case sensitive. gss_accept_delegation defaults to off, meaning credentials from the client are not accepted. oauth_validator_libraries defaults to an empty string, which refuses OAuth connections; if only one validator library is provided, it is used by default for any OAuth connections, otherwise all oauth HBA entries must explicitly set a validator chosen from this list. Validator modules must be implemented or obtained separately; PostgreSQL does not ship with any default implementations. The page says the parameters for transfer encryption using TLS protocols are named ssl for historic reasons, even though support for the SSL protocol has been deprecated, and that SSL is used interchangeably with TLS in this context. ssl defaults to off. ssl_ca_file defaults to empty, meaning no CA file is loaded and client certificate verification is not performed. ssl_cert_file defaults to server.crt. ssl_crl_file defaults to empty, meaning no CRL file is loaded unless ssl_crl_dir is set. ssl_crl_dir defaults to empty, meaning no CRLs are used unless ssl_crl_file is set; the directory must be prepared with the OpenSSL command openssl rehash or c_rehash. With ssl_crl_dir, CRLs are loaded on demand at connection time, and new CRLs added to the directory are used immediately; this differs from ssl_crl_file, which loads the CRL at server start time or when the configuration is reloaded. Both settings can be used together. ssl_key_file defaults to server.key. ssl_tls13_ciphers, if left blank, uses the default set in OpenSSL. ssl_ciphers defaults to HIGH:MEDIUM:+3DES:!aNULL; the page explains that HIGH means cipher suites that use ciphers from the HIGH group, such as AES, Camellia and 3DES; MEDIUM means cipher suites that use ciphers from the MEDIUM group, such as RC4 and SEED; +3DES reorders 3DES after all other HIGH and MEDIUM ciphers because the OpenSSL default order puts 3DES higher than AES128, which the page calls wrong because 3DES offers less security than AES128 and is much slower; !aNULL disables anonymous cipher suites that do no authentication, which are vulnerable to MITM attacks. ssl_prefer_server_ciphers defaults to on; PostgreSQL versions before 9.4 do not have this setting and always use the client's preferences. ssl_groups defaults to X25519:prime256v1; in PostgreSQL versions before 18.0 this setting was named ssl_ecdh_curve and accepted only a single value. ssl_min_protocol_version defaults to TLSv1.2, which the page says satisfies industry best practices as of this writing; valid values are TLSv1, TLSv1.1, TLSv1.2 and TLSv1.3; protocol versions before TLS 1.0, namely SSL version 2 and 3, are always disabled. ssl_max_protocol_version defaults to allowing any version; valid values are the same as for ssl_min_protocol_version, plus an empty string. ssl_dh_params_file defaults to empty, in which case compiled-in default DH parameters are used; using custom DH parameters reduces exposure if an attacker cracks the well-known compiled-in DH parameters. ssl_passphrase_command defaults to empty, which means the built-in prompting mechanism is used; the command must print the passphrase to standard output and exit with code 0; in the parameter value, %p is replaced by a prompt string, and %% writes a literal %; a single newline is stripped from the end of the output if present. ssl_passphrase_command_supports_reload defaults to off; if off, the command is ignored during a reload and the SSL configuration is not reloaded if a passphrase is needed; this is appropriate for a command that requires a TTY for prompting, which might not be available when the server is running; setting it to on might be appropriate if the passphrase is obtained from a file; the page says this parameter must be set to on when running on Windows, because all connections perform a configuration reload due to the different process model of that platform. The page header also shows a release notice dated October 15, 2026: "PostgreSQL 19 RC 1 Released!" That notice is separate from the settings text. The page states defaults and rules for PostgreSQL 18, and refers to other sections and chapters for more detail, such as Chapter 20 for client authentication, Section 18.9 for SSL setup, Section 20.5 for password details, Section 20.6 for Kerberos, and Chapter 50 for implementing OAuth validators. It gives no measured performance numbers or comparisons between PostgreSQL versions, except for the noted changes in ssl_groups and ssl_prefer_server_ciphers.

The azure source describes a server-side pool built into the managed service. PgBouncer is an optional, built-in connection pool for Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible servers. It is supported on General Purpose and Memory Optimized compute tiers, in both public and private access networks, and is not supported on the Burstable tier. It runs on the same virtual machine as the database server. The deployed version is 1.25.2. It listens on port 6432; the normal PostgreSQL port is 5432. Applications connect to the same host name but change the port to 6432. The source states PgBouncer is enabled by default on port 6432, and also says you enable it by setting the parameter pgbouncer.enabled to true in the Parameters pane; no server restart is needed. These two statements about the default state sit together in the source and are not reconciled there. Key numbers and defaults: pgbouncer.default_pool_size = 50 server connections per user/database pair; pgbouncer.max_client_conn = 5000 maximum client connections; pgbouncer.max_prepared_statements = 0; pgbouncer.min_pool_size = 0; pgbouncer.pool_mode = transaction; pgbouncer.query_wait_timeout = 120 seconds; pgbouncer.server_idle_timeout = 600 seconds. The source says PgBouncer can scale to up to 10,000 connections with low overhead, and that PostgreSQL itself runs into resource constraints above a few thousand connections. It recommends transaction pooling for most users. It states that statement pool mode cannot be used with prepared statements, and that prepared-statement support in transaction mode is turned on by setting max_prepared_statements above its default of 0; this applies only to protocol-level prepared statements, such as those sent through the libpq PQprepare function, not to text commands like PREPARE proc AS. PgBouncer metrics are disabled by default; to use them, enable pgbouncer.enabled and metrics.pgbouncer_diagnostics; both are dynamic and need no restart. Metrics are emitted every one minute and kept for up to 93 days. The metric list includes active client connections, waiting client connections, active server connections, idle server connections, total pooled connections, number of connection pools, and a preview metric for total client connections. Metrics that use the DatabaseName dimension have a 30-database limit, applied to the OID column in creation order. Logs go to the AzureDiagnostics table (Category == "PostgreSQLFlexPGBouncer") or the PGSQLPgBouncer table, depending on schema. An admin database named pgbouncer allows SHOW commands such as SHOW HELP, SHOW POOLS, SHOW DATABASES and SHOW STATS; access requires setting pgbouncer.stats_users. PgBouncer restarts whenever the server restarts, including scale operations and HA failover, so existing connections must be re-established. In zone-redundant high availability, PgBouncer runs on the primary and restarts on the newly promoted standby after failover, so the application connection string does not change. For elastic clusters, each node has its own PgBouncer; port 6432 routes to the coordinator node and port 8432 routes to worker nodes. The source calls PgBouncer a potential single point of failure and suggests multiple instances behind a load balancer on Azure VMs as a mitigation. It notes PgBouncer is single-threaded, which may limit scaling for many short-lived connections, and names PgCat as a multithreaded alternative on Azure VMs. The parameter pgbouncer.client_tls_sslmode is deprecated; when require_secure_transport is ON, TLS is automatically enforced for built-in PgBouncer, and this is on by default for new servers. The portal does not show all PgBouncer parameters until you leave and reopen the Parameters pane. You can change the timeout for one request. Pass timeout=10.0 to wait 10 seconds, or timeout=None to turn timeouts off. You can also set a default on a client: httpx.Client() keeps the 5-second default, httpx.Client(timeout=10.0) uses 10 seconds, and httpx.Client(timeout=None) disables timeouts by default. These examples come from the same source (original-1).

HTTPX also lets you tune four separate timeout types. A connect timeout limits the wait for a socket connection to the host; if it fails, HTTPX raises ConnectTimeout. A read timeout limits the wait for a chunk of received data, such as part of the response body; if it fails, HTTPX raises ReadTimeout. A write timeout limits the wait to send a chunk of data, such as part of the request body; if it fails, HTTPX raises WriteTimeout. A pool timeout limits the wait to get a connection from the connection pool; if it fails, HTTPX raises PoolTimeout. The maximum number of connections in the pool is set by the limits argument. The source gives this example: httpx.Timeout(10.0, connect=60.0) means a 60-second connect timeout and a 10-second timeout for the other types (original-1).
